paras: The lynching of Willie Johns was the shooting of a young man accused of robbing and burning a store in Coffee County, Georgia, whose body was found at Indian Ford shortly before April 5, 1881. Johns had been placed in the custody of five men; two of them told a coroner's inquest that armed men had taken him from them, and the jury found that he died at the hands of "an unknown party or parties." A Georgia weekly reported the killing as a lynching, and an Atlanta dispatch carried it to Northern papers under headlines such as "Mob Law in Georgia" and "Lynched by Fiends."

Some time earlier, a store in Coffee County was robbed and then burned; the Atlanta dispatch named its owner as Daniel or Dan Potts, while the Berrien County News called him "Mr. Dan Lott." Suspicion fell on Willie Johns, described in the dispatch as a young man, who was accused of the crime, seized, and placed in the custody of five men. None of the reports gives Johns's race.

According to the Berrien County News, the men had charge of the prisoner when he left Dixonia. What became of him was unknown until a party of hunters found his body at Indian Ford, which most versions of the dispatch placed on Seventeen Mile Creek and one on Mill Creek. The shorter dispatch said he was found five days after he was taken away, with his head shot to pieces and part of his brain clutched in one hand. The Berrien County News called the sight "a most horrible and sickening one," and reported that a family living near the ford had heard five guns fired in its direction "one day last week" and taken it for a hunting party.

How Johns left his guards' hands is known only from the guards themselves, who said that an armed body of men met them on the road, overpowered them and took the prisoner away. A rumor repeated by both the Georgia paper and the wire held that these unknown men took Johns to Indian Ford and shot him there.

According to the Atlanta dispatch, two of the five men who had taken Johns away were arrested once the body was found and brought before the coroner, where both swore they knew nothing of his fate. The coroner's jury returned a verdict that Johns "came to his death at the hands of an unknown party or parties." No report of further arrests, an indictment or a trial was found.

In Georgia, the Savannah Morning News printed the news on April 5 in its column of state items, quoting the Berrien County News under the plain statement that Johns "has been lynched." The Atlanta dispatch, dated April 7 (April 8 in one version), appeared from April 8 in the Chicago Daily Tribune, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the Wheeling Register and the Daily Gazette, and as late as April 20 in the Somerset Herald of Pennsylvania. These papers framed the killing in terms of Southern law, heading it "A Horrible Usurpation of the Law," "Mob Law in Georgia," "Georgia Justice" and "Southern Idea of What Should Be."

The Daily Gazette went furthest, titling its version "Lynched by Fiends" over the subhead "Shot to Pieces for Robbing and Burning a Store," while the Wheeling Register's subhead called it murder "by a Mob." Beneath these headlines the dispatch itself offered no comment, and like the Georgia report it did not mention race.

The reports differ on the storekeeper's name, Potts in the wire and Lott in the Berrien County News, and on whether Indian Ford lay on Seventeen Mile Creek or Mill Creek. Dispatches dated April 7 and 8 said the body had been found "to-day," although the Savannah paper had already printed the inquest verdict on April 5, which suggests the wire carried older news. Only the wire reports that two guards were arrested, and the account that an armed band seized Johns rests on those guards' own testimony and on rumor.
